debates.motion: Does the Kalam cosmological argument show that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator?

sections.title: Causation, Nothingness, and an Eternal Material Alternative
sections.rationale: This opening section follows the exchange over the Kalam’s causal premise, the disanalogy between ordinary and cosmic beginnings, and the proposed alternative of an eternal material series. Its 16 percent weight reflects the structural role of causation without displacing the debate’s larger finitude and creator exchanges.

sections.title: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
sections.rationale: This section gathers the first finitude argument and the sustained Hilbert’s Hotel exchange over part-whole intuitions, inconsistent principles, checkout cases, and relative complements. Its 27 percent weight reflects the breadth and central structural role of the actual-infinite route and its detailed opposition.

sections.title: Successive Addition, Countdown, and Descending-Series Paradoxes
sections.rationale: This section contains the second finitude argument and the extended dispute over whether a beginningless sequence can terminate in the present. It includes the conditional, explanatory-timing, and Grim Reaper exchanges. Its 27 percent weight parallels the independent actual-infinite route’s structural scope.

sections.title: Metric Time and the Scope of Temporal Beginning
sections.rationale: This compact section isolates the late clarification about what the finitude arguments establish: a beginning of metric time and the possible status of a non-metric or amorphous temporal reality. Its 10 percent weight recognizes a consequential scope issue while preserving proportion with the fuller exchanges.

sections.title: Impersonal Indeterminism and Timeless Personal Agency
sections.rationale: This final section organizes the creator inference, the impersonal indeterministic alternative, and the dispute over whether changeless consciousness is coherent. Its 20 percent weight reflects the separate and explicit personhood component of the motion while retaining the earlier causal and finitude emphasis.

routes.description: The defender’s route applies the causal principle to a universe whose finite temporal beginning is established by arguments against an actual infinite and against formation by successive addition, then identifies a personal agent as the best explanation of the universe’s first effect.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that the past is finite, that the universe consequently began and has a cause, and that an eternal impersonal mechanism cannot explain a temporally first universe whereas personal agency can.

bridges.description: The Kalam shows that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
A beginningless past would contain an actually infinite number of events; because such an actual infinite cannot exist, the temporal series and universe began.
Hilbert-style concrete scenarios reveal that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible, despite the consistency of infinite set theory.
An actually infinite temporal series cannot be formed by successive addition or completed by counting down from a beginningless past.
An eternal impersonal cause would produce its effect eternally or not at all, while a personal agent can freely originate a temporally first universe.

routes.description: The critic’s route argues that the Kalam does not exclude a beginningless material reality and that its paradoxes and conceptual analysis leave coherent infinite-past and impersonal-cause alternatives available.
routes.successCriteria: Show that actual-infinite scenarios establish strangeness rather than impossibility, that successive-addition reasoning does not rule out a beginningless series ending in the present, or that an impersonal indeterministic cause can explain a first universe without a personal creator.

bridges.description: The Kalam does not show that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
The Kalam’s finitude and personhood inferences fail to exclude coherent beginningless-past or impersonal-origin alternatives, so its conclusion is not established.
The unusual behavior of Hilbert’s Hotel does not entail that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible.
The impossibility of reaching the end of an endless count does not establish the impossibility of reaching the present end of a beginningless countdown.
An impersonal indeterministic cause could originate the universe at one time, so a personal cause is not uniquely required.

moves.sectionTitle: Causation, Nothingness, and an Eternal Material Alternative
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Everything that begins to exist has a cause because being cannot arise from nothing, a principle Craig regards as more evident than premises offered to prove it.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The causal route is intelligible but chiefly intuitive and overconfident; the unsupported motive attribution materially tests charity.

moves.sectionTitle: Causation, Nothingness, and an Eternal Material Alternative
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Ordinary caused beginnings merely rearrange existing material and therefore provide no observed analogue or inductive support for an absolute beginning of material reality.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The ordinary-versus-absolute-beginning distinction directly contests empirical support but leaves the independent metaphysical intuition unanswered.

moves.sectionTitle: Causation, Nothingness, and an Eternal Material Alternative
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Prior’s principle concerns substances rather than events, and the universe’s absolute beginning strengthens the need for a transcendent cause because no prior nature could discriminate which thing appears.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply contacts both the substance distinction and the alleged significance of an absolute beginning, though its discriminatory-nothingness warrant remains weak.

moves.sectionTitle: Causation, Nothingness, and an Eternal Material Alternative
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Paraphrasing claims about nothingness into quantified language does not explain why a substance cannot begin uncaused and risks presupposing the causal principle under dispute.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The linguistic objection challenges the causal principle but does not fully answer the separate discrimination argument about why one substance appears.

moves.sectionTitle: Causation, Nothingness, and an Eternal Material Alternative
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: If nothing comes from nothing and something exists now, then something must always have existed, which Malpass takes to favor an eternal material causal series rather than a first beginning.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The modus-tollens step supports always-existing reality, but the further leap to eternal materiality and a causal chain is underwarranted.

moves.sectionTitle: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A beginningless temporal series would instantiate an actually infinite number of past events; because an actual infinite cannot exist in reality, the past is finite and the universe began to exist.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: This constructive states its own actual-infinite route without representing or attacking a developed live alternative, so charity is untested.

moves.sectionTitle: Successive Addition, Countdown, and Descending-Series Paradoxes
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because a temporal series is formed by adding events successively and an actual infinite cannot be formed that way, the past must be finite and have a beginning.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Charity is untested, while the inference leaves a material ambiguity between a beginningless series and an infinite formed from a starting point.

moves.sectionTitle: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Hilbert’s fully occupied infinite hotel can continually accommodate infinitely many guests, illustrating why actual infinities belong to mathematical thought rather than concrete reality.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The move presents its own Hilbert illustration without engaging a live alternative; its route is intelligible but retains a material bridge from strangeness to impossibility.

moves.sectionTitle: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Hilbert’s Hotel would behave strangely by accommodating new guests despite every room being occupied, but that strangeness is insufficient to establish that such a hotel could not exist.

moves.sectionTitle: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Finite intuitions such as Euclid’s maxim need not govern infinite collections, where proper subsets can be equinumerous with their wholes, so mathematical strangeness does not establish metaphysical impossibility.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The excerpt identifies the illicit transfer of finite intuitions and explains why infinite equinumerosity defeats the claimed impossibility inference.

moves.sectionTitle: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Metaphysical intuition is legitimate even in Malpass’s own principles, and rejecting concrete actual infinities preserves both part-whole inequality and one-to-one equinumerosity.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Specific opposing principles substantiate the legitimacy of metaphysical intuition, although they do not independently settle which member of the triad to reject.

moves.sectionTitle: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: The inconsistent triad can be handled linguistically by distinguishing how terms and principles apply in infinite contexts, avoiding a substantive commitment that actual infinities are impossible.

moves.sectionTitle: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Removing equally infinite groups from Hilbert's Hotel can leave different remainders, which Craig regards as persuasive evidence that concrete actual infinities generate unacceptable inverse-operation results.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The checkout examples partially pressure the linguistic resolution but do not directly defeat its context-sensitive treatment of infinite collections.

moves.sectionTitle: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Hilbert’s checkout cases can be represented by relative complements in set theory, which return determinate remaining sets without contradiction; the subtraction formulation is therefore misleading.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The response precisely diagnoses pseudo-subtraction and states the defeating consequence: relative complements yield determinate remainders without contradiction.

moves.sectionTitle: Actual Infinities and Hilbert’s Hotel
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Relative-complement language does not remove the concrete arithmetic problem: removing equal infinite quantities can leave unequal remainders, even if formal transfinite arithmetic prohibits the operation.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The wording is understandable but materially blurs equal cardinalities, identical subsets, ordinary subtraction, and formal transfinite operations.

moves.sectionTitle: Successive Addition, Countdown, and Descending-Series Paradoxes
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: The impossibility of reaching the end of an endless upward count does not transfer to a beginningless countdown that has a terminal event, so the symmetry-based successive-addition inference fails.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply diagnoses the count-up/countdown asymmetry and its defeating consequence, but it does not separately answer every component of the successive-addition case.

moves.sectionTitle: Successive Addition, Countdown, and Descending-Series Paradoxes
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: If a beginningless countdown could finish today, it could have finished at any earlier past point; then the counter could never be found counting, contradicting the hypothesis that the countdown occurred.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The move structurally diagnoses a contradiction in finishing today, but its inference wrongly treats infinite prior duration as sufficient for earlier completion.

moves.sectionTitle: Successive Addition, Countdown, and Descending-Series Paradoxes
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Craig reverses the conditional: infinitely much elapsed time is necessary, not sufficient, for completing the countdown, so having enough time does not entail that the counter had already finished yesterday.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The response exceptionally reconstructs the necessary-versus-sufficient-condition issue and preserves the distinction between could, should, and would.

moves.sectionTitle: Successive Addition, Countdown, and Descending-Series Paradoxes
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The unexplained timing of a beginningless countdown requires only a restricted, case-specific principle of sufficient reason, not a controversial universal principle.

moves.sectionTitle: Successive Addition, Countdown, and Descending-Series Paradoxes
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: The counter's rate and immediately preceding number partially explain why the count ends today; requiring an ultimate explanation would reinstate a stronger and disputable PSR.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The rate and preceding number provide a concrete partial explanation, while the contrast with an ultimate explanation supports the stated PSR objection.

moves.sectionTitle: Successive Addition, Countdown, and Descending-Series Paradoxes
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A partial explanation must identify the contextually relevant explanatory factor, and citing yesterday's preceding number leaves the counter's completion today no less mysterious.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Contextual causal examples support the relevance objection, and the conclusion is appropriately qualified as leaving the timing no less mysterious.

moves.sectionTitle: Successive Addition, Countdown, and Descending-Series Paradoxes
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A beginningless sequence of progressively earlier Grim Reapers implies both that the victim cannot survive midnight and that no Reaper can kill the victim, producing a contradiction from the descending series.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The stipulated Reaper case yields its local contradiction, but the move compresses the bridge from that setup to descending temporal series generally.

moves.sectionTitle: Metric Time and the Scope of Temporal Beginning
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Even granting the actual-infinite and successive-addition arguments, they may establish only a beginning of metric time while permitting a beginningless non-metric temporal reality.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The move justifiably narrows the conclusion to metric time and supplies a non-metric replacement possibility, though that possibility is only lightly defended.

moves.sectionTitle: Metric Time and the Scope of Temporal Beginning
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Craig acknowledges that his argument directly establishes a beginning only for metric time and grants that amorphous pre-metric time is possible, while arguing it would resemble timelessness and is not the best explanation.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The metric and amorphous-time distinction is recoverable, but the claims about geometric structure, a point, and timelessness remain compressed.

moves.sectionTitle: Impersonal Indeterminism and Timeless Personal Agency
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: An indeterministic impersonal mechanism could happen to initiate time, and its unexplained timing resembles libertarian free choice closely enough that personal agency is not uniquely required.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The indeterministic mechanism and libertarian-choice analogy supplies a relevant conceptual alternative, but its explanatory mechanism remains materially underdeveloped.

moves.sectionTitle: Impersonal Indeterminism and Timeless Personal Agency
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because no scientifically plausible impersonal indeterministic account explains why a nonphysical state produced the universe only finitely long ago, the universe’s origin is best explained by a personal agent.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply contacts scientific plausibility and finite timing but leaves the agency-mechanism similarity unresolved, while overstating the eternity-or-never claim.

moves.sectionTitle: Impersonal Indeterminism and Timeless Personal Agency
moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Consciousness appears essentially dynamic, so a wholly changeless and disembodied mind outside a changing causal order may be incoherent.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The timeless-agent concern is represented fairly overall, but the freeze model omits a decisive distinction between absent experience and persisting changeless consciousness.

moves.sectionTitle: Impersonal Indeterminism and Timeless Personal Agency
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The freeze illustration supports unperceived changeless consciousness rather than refuting it, and a timeless person, though unlike an ordinary person, is not incoherent.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The response covers the experiential illustration and incoherence conclusion, but unawareness does not establish persisting changeless consciousness and the remaining support is asserted.

debates.motion: Is belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God rational given alleged gratuitous evil, salvation confusion, rationality, design, and morality?

sections.title: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
sections.rationale: Beginning with the debate’s definition of rational belief, this section groups the competing accounts of why human cognition can be trusted and the ensuing exchange over evolutionary truth-tracking and theistic reliability.

sections.title: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
sections.rationale: This section collects the initial evidential challenge from apparently purposeless suffering, the evil-God comparison, the concession about its significance, and the principal theistic accounts of normativity, afterlife, theodicy, and divine participation in suffering.

sections.title: Salvation Confusion and the Identity of God
sections.rationale: This section connects the critique of disputed salvation conditions with the cumulative case for rational theism and the later contention that generic creator arguments do not by themselves identify an all-powerful, all-loving religious God.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning and Evolutionary Accounts of Design
sections.rationale: This section places the cosmic fine-tuning argument alongside the later evolutionary account of apparent biological design, preserving the debate’s distinct but related explanations of ordered and life-permitting features.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: This section groups the moral argument for God, the evolutionary account of moral intuitions, and the extended exchange over whether goodness is independent of God, arbitrarily commanded, or grounded in the divine nature.

routes.description: Establish that belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational because the available evidence includes apparently gratuitous evil and confused salvation requirements, while the proposed arguments from reason, design, and morality do not adequately support that God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the conflict between the claimed divine attributes and the observed world, together with epistemic and salvation confusion, defeats or outweighs the cumulative positive case for rational theism.

bridges.description: Given the available reason and evidence, belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God is irrational.

Apparently gratuitous evil and related epistemic confusion outweigh the proposed arguments for God and prevent those arguments from rationally supporting the all-powerful, all-loving God under discussion.
Pervasive suffering that appears to serve no greater good is improbable under an all-powerful, all-loving God, and merely possible theodicies do not make belief in that God rational.
An all-loving God would not attach grave eternal consequences to salvation conditions that sincere people cannot reliably identify and religious communities cannot agree upon.

Evolutionary accounts of cognition and morality, together with alternative explanations of apparent design, undercut the claim that reason, fine-tuning, or moral experience rationally identifies the proposed God.

routes.description: Establish that belief in God is rational through a cumulative case from the reliability of reason, the life-permitting structure of the universe, and objective morality, while answering the evidential challenge from suffering.
routes.successCriteria: Show that rationality, design, and morality are collectively more expected or intelligible if God exists than if God does not, and that suffering does not defeat this cumulative support.

bridges.description: The cumulative available evidence makes belief in God more rational than nonbelief.

The combined evidence from rational minds, cosmic design, and objective morality makes God more probable than God's nonexistence, while available responses prevent suffering from defeating that inference.
Unguided naturalism undermines confidence that evolved minds track truth, whereas an intelligent creator provides a rational basis for trusting human reason and the universe's intelligibility.
The universe's highly specific life-permitting conditions are substantially more probable under intelligent design than under an unguided chance hypothesis.
Objective moral obligations are difficult to ground in an impersonal, purposeless universe but are intelligible when goodness is grounded in God.

moves.sectionTitle: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: A belief is rational when it accords with the reason and evidence available to the believer; rationality and truth are therefore distinct questions.

moves.sectionTitle: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: The world appears filled with suffering that serves no greater good, while belief in an all-powerful, all-loving God requires denying that any such gratuitous evil exists.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The inference is clear and fairly states the classical commitment, but examples of suffering do not establish gratuity, and the emphatic certainty exceeds the supplied warrant.

moves.sectionTitle: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: An evil-God hypothesis can reconcile apparent goodness with maximal evil as readily as theodicies reconcile apparent evil with perfect goodness, showing that a merely possible reconciliation does not make either hypothesis probable or rational.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The evil-God analogy directly advances the subsidiary burden, while its probabilistic symmetry remains asserted rather than fully defended.

moves.sectionTitle: Salvation Confusion and the Identity of God
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: An all-loving God would not impose grave or eternal consequences for lacking salvation while Christians, Muslims, and Jews cannot reliably agree on which disputed beliefs salvation requires.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The examples provide some support and directly establish the subsidiary issue, but broad prevalence claims and omitted inclusivist qualifications materially limit the move.

moves.sectionTitle: Salvation Confusion and the Identity of God
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: An all-loving God would not create a salvation 'hoop' that appears unlikely, is disputed even by believers, and remains invisible to people who then face eternal punishment.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The salvation-hoop formulation directly develops the necessary subsidiary burden and connects disputed conditions, invisibility, and punishment.

moves.sectionTitle: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: If minds result only from mindless, unguided physical processes, confidence in their truth-tracking is self-undermining, whereas an intelligent creator explains why minds and the universe are intelligible.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The span materially narrows atheism to a physicalist, unguided account, though the reconstruction is not so extreme as the lower candidate implies.

moves.sectionTitle: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Natural selection favors advantageous behavior rather than truth, creating a self-undermining reliability problem for unguided evolution that guided evolution avoids because God would intend rational knowers.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The move directly develops the subsidiary route, but it jumps from selection for behavior to general unreliability and relies chiefly on assertion and authority.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning and Evolutionary Accounts of Design
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: The universe’s physical properties occupy extraordinarily narrow life-permitting ranges whose occurrence by chance is effectively implausible, while their apparent calibration is naturally explained by a super-intellect.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Specific constants, magnitudes, and an analogy supply some support, but the chance comparison and design warrant remain substantially undefended.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Objective moral wrongs require explanation, and God is the best explanation because denying objective morality conflicts with deep moral judgments while atheism must otherwise ground moral law without God.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The stated alternatives omit important secular accounts but still preserve the basic distinction between denying objectivity and grounding it without God.

moves.sectionTitle: Salvation Confusion and the Identity of God
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: The arguments from rationality, design, and morality cumulatively make God's existence more probable than God's nonexistence and therefore make belief in God more rational than the alternative.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: This is an untested summary of the speaker's own case; combining three compressed arguments does not by itself establish independence, probability, or cumulative force.

moves.sectionTitle: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Attacking atheism does not establish theism; Edwards also conflates atheism with naturalism and has not shown why evolution would favor costly false beliefs over broadly accurate ones.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply contacts the scope error, the comparative inference, and the selection-to-truth warrant, but it omits guided evolution and overstates the target's atheism-naturalism identification.

moves.sectionTitle: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Evolution need not make cognition wholly unreliable because false representations are often costly, so selection can favor broadly accurate beliefs even though human access to truth remains imperfect.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply contacts the evolutionary target's reliability components but not its guided alternative; its broad-truth conclusion is qualified yet rests on an underdefended cost premise.

moves.sectionTitle: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Theism treats truth as the intended function of human reason, while evolutionary success only sometimes correlates with truth and therefore supplies a weaker basis for trust.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply accurately presents the opposing claim that truth often aids evolutionary success while preserving the decisive qualification that correlation need not be constant.

moves.sectionTitle: Rational Belief and the Reliability of Human Reason
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Theism suffers an analogous reliability problem because believers lack access to God’s supposedly mysterious reasoning and must trust that God implanted their access to truth; a shared defect cannot favor theism over naturalism.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The move identifies the alleged parallel reliability defect and separately states its defeating comparative consequence, while representing the creator-based account with only bounded compression.

moves.sectionTitle: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Suffering and evil are probably the strongest counterevidence to an all-powerful, all-loving God, although Simon denies that they defeat theism.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The concession coherently recognizes evidential pressure but neither addresses apparent gratuity nor the attribute conflict; the asserted availability of answers is unsupported here.

moves.sectionTitle: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Christianity affirms the intuition that suffering makes the world other than it ought to be, whereas an atheistic universe of blind indifference cannot affirm that normative judgment.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The claim that atheism cannot affirm a normative judgment substitutes cosmic purpose for the strongest secular moral position and materially weakens the alternative.

moves.sectionTitle: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Assessment of earthly suffering must include an eternal future in which God has resources to restore sufferers and wipe away every tear.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Afterlife restoration is clearly and fairly offered as relevant counterpressure, but compensation is not bridged to the absence of gratuitous suffering and rests on scriptural assurance.

moves.sectionTitle: Gratuitous Evil, Theodicy, and Restoration
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: Recognized defenses involving the best possible world, free will, and soul-making offer serious responses to evil, while Christianity additionally holds that God entered human suffering and can strengthen sufferers and agents who help them.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The span names theodicies and pastoral claims without explaining how they answer gratuity or the evil-God parity, while its authority-based reconstruction weakens the actual probability challenge.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Evolution in a social species explains care, sacrifice, moral intuitions, and the emotional force of religious motifs without requiring theism.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: A causal account of moral intuitions is relevant but does not contact the target's normative affirmation claim, and calling it complete overstates both its reach and warrant.

moves.sectionTitle: Salvation Confusion and the Identity of God
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Even granting arguments for a creator, the conflict between an all-powerful, all-loving God and the world's suffering prevents identifying that creator with the Christian God or Allah.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The move justifies replacing generic-creator support with the motion's identity demand and answers that demand through the attribute conflict, though the conflict's evidential premise remains compressed.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: If God follows independently good standards, morality does not depend on God; if God's commands define goodness, morality becomes arbitrary authority, as troubling scriptural commands illustrate.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Both horns directly contact the claimed need for a divine ground and the possibility of independence, making coverage complete despite compressed support for the scriptural illustrations.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: The moral standards used to condemn biblical practices were themselves historically advanced by the Bible's teaching that every person bears God's image and therefore has value and dignity.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Historical moral influence supplies related contrary material but answers neither horn of the dilemma, while recasting the cited commands as a few obscure passages materially weakens the target.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
moves.speaker: Simon Edwards
moves.proposition: The divine-command dilemma is avoided because God neither obeys an external good nor arbitrarily creates goodness: God is the good, and objective value is grounded in the personal creator who set everything in motion.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The dilemma is reconstructed accurately, but identifying the creator with goodness and asking who else could qualify does not defend the proposed grounding against arbitrariness.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Evolution, and Divine Goodness
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Identifying God with goodness only restates the dilemma: either God aligns with an independently existing standard or God defines goodness by existing, leaving morality as mere conformity to God.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply restates the dilemma against the identity proposal but offers little warrant for why identifying God with goodness cannot constitute a distinct account.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning and Evolutionary Accounts of Design
moves.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moves.proposition: Before evolutionary theory, biological complexity could rationally suggest creation, but convergent evolutionary evidence now supplies a natural account of apparent design and makes special creation unnecessary even if God could have used evolution.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Evolution directly supplies the required subsidiary alternative to apparent biological design, but the asserted convergent evidence is not made specific within the selected span.

debates.motion: Does the evidence from cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, Jesus' resurrection, and religious experience make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism?

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
sections.rationale: This opening section follows the earliest exchange from the universe's beginning and causal explanation through the proposed attributes and personality of its cause, including the later scientific, causal, and infinity-focused replies. Its weight reflects the number and structural depth of the linked cosmological steps.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity
sections.rationale: This section begins with the fine-tuning constructive and follows the exchange over cosmic probabilities, deeper physics, multiverse alternatives, and what properties a designer inference could establish. The weight represents a distinct evidential line with several independent structural questions.

sections.title: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil
sections.rationale: This section starts with the moral constructive, then groups the exchange over whether objective value requires God, how naturalism might ground value and obligation, and whether evil fits a perfect deity. Its weight reflects the interaction between a positive moral line and a distinct contrary-evidence line.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Sources
sections.rationale: This section isolates the resurrection line because it turns on a distinctive historical record: the empty tomb, appearances, disciples' belief, source dependence, discrepancies, and historian agreement. Its weight reflects an independent route to specifically Christian theism with a compact direct exchange.

sections.title: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden
sections.rationale: This final section begins with personal religious experience and follows the chronological exchange over religious disagreement, competing hypotheses, the required comparative case, and absence-of-evidence reasoning. Its weight reflects its role in connecting one evidential line to the debate's cumulative and motion-level framing.

routes.description: A cumulative Christian-theist route arguing that cosmological origins, fine-tuning, objective morality, Jesus' resurrection, and personal religious experience jointly favor the Christian God over skeptical atheism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cited evidence is established, its principal naturalistic alternatives are inadequate, and its combined explanatory force makes the specifically Christian God more reasonable than skeptical atheism.

bridges.description: The evidence from cosmology, fine-tuning, morality, Jesus' resurrection, and religious experience makes Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism.
The cumulative convergence of the five evidential lines supplies good reason to accept Christian theism and no comparably good reason to accept atheism.
The universe's finite beginning and need for a cause imply an uncaused, timeless, spaceless, immaterial transcendent cause.
The universe's life-permitting fine-tuning is better explained by intelligent design than by physical necessity or chance.
The empty tomb, post-mortem appearances, and origin of the disciples' resurrection belief are best explained by God raising Jesus from the dead.

routes.description: A skeptical-atheist route arguing that the proposed evidence is uncertain, underdetermines the Christian God, admits natural alternatives, and conflicts with what would be expected from an omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect being.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the principal theistic inferences lack adequate evidential support or specificity and the observed world is at least as expected under skeptical atheism as under the Christian God hypothesis.

bridges.description: The cited evidence does not make Christian theism more reasonable than skeptical atheism and instead supports withholding or rejecting belief in the Christian God.
The five proposed evidential lines fail to meet the strong burden required for the specific Christian God hypothesis because their inferences are underdetermined and face contrary empirical evidence.
The Kalam inference is inadequately supported because ordinary causal experience does not establish causation for creation ex nihilo or for the physical universe as a whole.
Fine-tuning probabilities are epistemically uncertain, admit deeper physical or multiverse explanations, and do not identify an omniperfect Christian God.
The world's evil and opaque divine presence are empirically less expected from a morally perfect Christian God than from skeptical atheism.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because the universe began to exist, it has a transcendent cause whose relation to time, space, and the causal regress requires it to be uncaused, timeless, changeless, spaceless, and immaterial.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The excerpt supplies an explicit causal route and reasons for the inferred attributes, though important cosmological warrants remain compressed.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A transcendent nonphysical cause must be an unembodied mind because the only alternative candidate, an abstract object, cannot stand in causal relations; therefore the universe has a personal creator.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The personal-cause inference is topical but rests on an unsupported exhaustive dichotomy; no live alternative position is materially represented.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Life-permitting fine-tuning is extraordinarily improbable under chance, is not physically necessary, exhibits an independent pattern, and therefore is best explained by design.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The categorical elimination of necessity and chance exceeds the excerpt's support and omits substantial uncertainty about the probability comparison.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values are evident in moral experience and, because they require God as their ground, their existence entails God's existence.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The moral syllogism remains intelligible despite a compressed grounding premise, while its constructive contribution lacks exact locked-route contact.

moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Sources
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Jesus' empty tomb, post-mortem appearances, and the disciples' unexpected resurrection belief lack a plausible naturalistic explanation and are best explained by God raising Jesus, thereby evidencing God's existence.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Named historical support gives the inference a useful evidential core, but the sweeping dismissal of natural explanations remains materially overstated.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A sincere seeker can know that God exists apart from argument through immediate personal experience, in which God is encountered as a directly given reality rather than merely adopted as an idea.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The move meaningfully develops the religious-experience line, but its universal assurance about sincere seekers is radically underwarranted.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Because mutually incompatible religions are acquired and maintained through similar sources such as upbringing, preaching, sacred texts, and religious experience, those methods are unreliable guides to truth.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply accurately distinguishes truth from belief acquisition and fairly identifies the similar sources underlying the live experience claim.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Even generously allowing disembodied mentality some prior probability, the specific omniperfect Christian God must compete with thousands of conflicting religious hypotheses, so absent an overwhelmingly strong case the rational conclusion is disbelief or at least agnosticism.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The specific Christian hypothesis is represented fairly, but the probability allocation and default move from agnosticism to atheism are overextended.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Ordinary causal experience concerns rearrangements of existing material and therefore does not justify extending the premise that whatever begins to exist has a cause to creation from nothing.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply states the causal argument accurately, expressly grants its validity, and isolates the strongest evidential challenge to its causal premise.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem establishes only a beginning to expansion, while contracting models and unresolved quantum-gravity problems prevent confidence in an absolute cosmic beginning.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The response accurately confines the theorem to past expansion and directly addresses the qualified scientific basis for a cosmic beginning.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: There is no evidence that minds exist without physical substrates, and even if the universe had a nonphysical cause it need not be an abstract object or mind but could be a kind of cause beyond evolved human comprehension.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The move diagnoses the false dichotomy and separately explains why an unknown nonphysical cause defeats the inference to an unembodied mind.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Religious disagreement does not discredit one common belief-forming method because religions do not share a single method, while Craig's own case uses logic, evidence, and personal experience.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply directly attacks the common-method premise and states its consequence, but it weakens the target's similar-method claim and offers little warrant for its scientific-method comparison.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The Borde-Guth-Vilenkin theorem still implies an absolute cosmic beginning, is independent of Einstein's gravitational equations and any quantum-gravity description, and therefore supplies strong cosmological evidence that the universe began.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The absence of observed creation from nothing does not undermine causation, because originating without either material or efficient cause would be still more absurd than originating without a material cause alone.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Calling causeless creation doubly impossible does not establish the needed extension from ordinary material rearrangement to creation ex nihilo.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: If the fundamental constants were shown to be physically inexplicable and precisely selected from a broad range of alternatives, that coincidence would naturally invite explanation by a cosmic designer.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The concession contacts only the conditioned design inference; the target separately contains probability, necessity, and pattern components.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning warrants caution because humans readily over-detect purpose, cosmic probability judgments rest on one observed universe, deeper physics may explain the constants, and a multiverse would make life-permitting observation unsurprising.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: Purpose-detection bias, probability uncertainty, deeper physics, and multiverse selection collectively contact all four indispensable fine-tuning components.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: Even established cosmic fine-tuning would not identify the morally perfect Christian God because the same life-enabling conditions are equally compatible with an evil or morally neutral designer.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The move supplies coherent symmetry-based specificity pressure while fairly treating fine-tuning as evidence for a designer rather than a complete cumulative case.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The nonunique result of subtracting infinity from infinity is not a contradiction but merely reflects that the inverse equation has multiple solutions, just as division of zero by zero is undefined without making zero incoherent.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The arithmetic explanation directly addresses a material infinity-based support for the cosmic-beginning premise, though it does not answer the whole causal route.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious Experience, Rival Hypotheses, and the Cumulative Burden
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Absence of evidence counts against God only if God's existence would make substantially more evidence probable, and Millican has supplied no grounds for that expectation beyond personal opinion.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply supplies a reasoned absence-of-evidence principle but contacts neither the rival-hypothesis dilution nor the target's default-belief conclusion.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmic Beginning, Causation, and a Personal Creator
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Millican's admission that infinite subtraction lacks a unique value is precisely the problem for a real collection, because physically removing equal infinite quantities from equal totals should not yield unequal remainders.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply explicitly diagnoses a real-world consequence and fully contacts the target, but its cardinal-arithmetic inference and confident contradiction claim remain defective.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning probabilities can be assessed by comparing possible parameter ranges with the narrow life-permitting range, diverse cases are unlikely all to disappear under future physics, and moral character is supplied by Craig's separate moral argument.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply clearly contacts three of five combined components with some support, but overstates the physics and compresses the purpose-bias and multiverse objections.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: An atheist can apprehend objective moral values without knowing their ultimate nature, and neither objective morality nor intrinsic human value evidently depends on God's existence.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: By accepting moral apprehension while directly challenging divine grounding, the reply contacts both indispensable components and represents the distinction fairly.

moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Sources
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The resurrection reports are late, non-eyewitness Christian advocacy documents; Matthew and Luke depend on Mark and another common source, and the accounts contain chronological and theological discrepancies, so they provide weak evidence for God.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The source criticism contacts only one of four historical-inference components and narrows the live case to gospel reports while omitting its broader support.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Naturalism supplies no nonarbitrary basis for privileging human or sentient flourishing and cannot explain binding moral obligations without a moral lawgiver.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply contacts grounding and intrinsic-value issues but substitutes a flourishing view for the target's broader atheist moral-realism position.

moves.sectionTitle: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Sources
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The three facts used in Craig's resurrection inference are accepted by a majority of historians, and even Millican's cited skeptical scholars accept the empty tomb, appearances, and origin of the disciples' belief.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The reply addresses only the discrepancy-related component and makes broader consensus claims with qualifications and support that remain incomplete.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil
moves.speaker: Peter Millican
moves.proposition: The observed world's evil and purported divine morality do not match expectations for a perfect God, so the evidence favors skepticism and provides strong evidence against God's existence with very little in favor.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The empirical evil argument directly counters the target's claim that evil supports rather than undermines the proposed divine moral ground.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-Tuning, Alternative Explanations, and Designer Specificity
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Fine-tuning and Craig's other presented arguments do not establish infinite power; at most they infer a being of enormous power, while an additional ontological argument would be needed for infinity.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The concession offers substantial specificity-related material about power but contacts neither moral-perfection component of the stated target.

moves.sectionTitle: Objective Morality, Divine Character, and the Evidence of Evil
moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Natural and moral evil may be permitted because God's purpose is to bring people freely into an eternal relationship with him, and an evil-containing world may maximize those who freely do so.

resolution.adjudicationRationale: The proposed link between an evil-containing world and maximizing freely chosen salvation is speculative and unsupported in the selected span.
